1. When copying Node-type properties, repairs are automatically applied based on the relative `NodePath`.
2. The `owner` property is also a Node-type property.

> 1. When copying Node-type properties, repairs are automatically applied based on the relative `NodePath`.
> 
>     2. The `owner` property is also a Node-type property.

Sorry if I'm misunderstanding something, but is this meant to be an explanation of why it's intended behaviour?

I don't really see how setting the owner property would cause the duplicate to become an instance instead of a copy. It just has the effect of making the new node permanently serialized within the test scene. And more importantly, it's called *after* calling `duplicate`.
Because if you copy it as is, it will produce errors. And what you want is **not to copy** the `owner`.

> Because if you copy it as is, it will produce errors. And what you want is **not to copy** the `owner`.

I still don't understand. I'm not copying any owner. I'm setting it.
`Node.duplicate()` copies the properties of the node. `owner` is not an exception.

> `Node.duplicate()` copies the properties of the node. `owner` is not an exception.

I'm not seeing the connection between owner and instance-ness. A non-instantiated node still can have an owner. And an instantiated node can have no owner.

If we were talking about the `scene_file_path` property I would understand.

Perhaps a better question is:

What does `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` even do then, and how do you actually duplicate a node without making it an instance?
You can use `propagate_call` to set `owner` to `null`.

> You can use `propagate_call` to set `owner` to `null`.

It's a single node that's being copied. There is no hierarchy. Please look at the project. Also setting owner to null (it's null by default anyway) means it doesn't even appear in the scene tree.

> > You can use `propagate_call` to set `owner` to `null`.
> 
> It's a single node that's being copied. There is no hierarchy. Please look at the project. Also setting owner to null (it's null by default anyway) means it doesn't even appear in the scene tree.

Yes, it is because `scene_file_path` is copied. This issue is about whether the scene icon in the scene tree should be displayed.

> Yes, it is because `scene_file_path` is copied. This issue is about whether the scene icon in the scene tree should be displayed.

No, I'm saying without setting `owner`, the duplicated node does not appear in the scene tree. I'm not talking about the icon.
Some nodes in the node tree may be removed over time. `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` will not remove these nodes immediately. It may make the node tree **structure** look like the initial state.

Anyway, it seems like the only workaround is to explicitly set `scene_file_path` on the duplicated node to an empty string.
However, this is the expected behaviour of leaving out `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION`. It should result in a node that:
- Does not have a `scene_file_path`
- Is not an instance of any scene

>  It should result in a node that:
> 
>     * Does not have a `scene_file_path`
> 
>     * Is not an instance of any scene

This sounds more like `DUPLICATE_NOT_AS_INSTANTIATION` .

> > It should result in a node that:
> > ```
> > * Does not have a `scene_file_path`
> > 
> > * Is not an instance of any scene
> > ```
> 
> This sounds more like `DUPLICATE_NOT_AS_INSTANTIATION` .

Yes... hence why I said "_leaving out DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION_".
It's included by default. But _leaving it out_ needs to make it _not_ use instantiation.
That's the whole premise of this bug report.

After the packed scene is instantiated, the scene instance is obtained.

We may have different understandings of **instantiation**: 
- you may think of instantiation as representing a scene instance;
- but in my opinion, instantiation here refers to the instantiation process. Do not use `PackedScene.instantiate()` when copy.

> After the packed scene is instantiated, the scene instance is obtained.
> 
> We may have different understandings of **instantiation**:
> 
>     * you may think of instantiation as representing a scene instance;
> 
>     * but in my opinion, instantiation here refers to the instantiation process. Do not use `PackedScene.instantiate()` when copy.

This might be so, but it isn't really useful to a user to know what function it uses behind the scenes if the expected _result_ is not achieved. The way the documentation describes this flag makes me think the _result_ would be whether or not something ends up being an instance. If this isn't the case, what is the result? What's the practical usage?

You can further configure the copied node tree to look like what you want. 

Although the configuration steps may be more cumbersome, the steps are less coupled, which provides more flexibility and freedom. You can combine the steps to create the desired results.

If you need to reset certain properties on the duplicated node that do not depend on the data used during the duplicate, there is no need to combine these setting steps into `duplicate()`.

The documentation explains `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` just fine.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2a9ff392645f1e1e073d937f1f6fb8feac896b2f/doc/classes/Node.xml#L1378-L1379


> If this isn't the case, what is the result? What's the practical usage?

`DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` is an extension flag, not a required flag. It extends the meaning of method `duplicate`, but it should not destroy the meaning of method `duplicate` if it is not used.

Duplicate a node and its properties, which is consistent with the meaning of duplicate. This is also the basic function of `duplicate()`. In other words, not copying certain properties is an extension feature.

> You can further configure the copied node tree to look like what you want.
> 
> Although the configuration steps may be more cumbersome, the steps are less coupled, which provides more flexibility and freedom. You can combine the steps to create the desired results.
> 
> If you need to reset certain properties on the duplicated node that do not depend on the data used during the duplicate, there is no need to combine these setting steps into `duplicate()`.
> 
> The documentation explains `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` just fine.
> 
> [godot/doc/classes/Node.xml](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2a9ff392645f1e1e073d937f1f6fb8feac896b2f/doc/classes/Node.xml#L1378-L1379)
> 
> Lines 1378 to 1379 in [2a9ff39](/godotengine/godot/commit/2a9ff392645f1e1e073d937f1f6fb8feac896b2f)
>  <constant name="DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION" value="8" enum="DuplicateFlags"> 
>  	Duplicate using [method PackedScene.instantiate]. If the node comes from a scene saved on disk, reuses [method PackedScene.instantiate] as the base for the duplicated node and its children. 
> 
> > If this isn't the case, what is the result? What's the practical usage?
> 
> `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` is an extension flag, not a required flag. It extends the meaning of method `duplicate`, but it should not destroy the meaning of method `duplicate` if it is not used.
> 
> Duplicate a node and its properties, which is consistent with the meaning of duplicate.

None of this answers the simple question of "why".

I know it's not a required flag, hence why I can leave it out. I can also appreciate the customizability of doing what you want post-duplication.

But again, what does leaving out this flag actually achieve? The documentation only says what function it uses behind the scenes, but it leaves it completely open to interpretation what the result is.

> `Node.duplicate()` copies the properties of the node. `owner` is not an exception.

Also just noting for the record that this is not true. Even though it has nothing to do with this bug report, still worth leaving a correction for anyone reading this in the future.

> But again, what does leaving out this flag actually achieve? The documentation only says what function it uses behind the scenes, but it leaves it completely open to interpretation what the result is.

The result is not described, but only the method used is described. This is because the method used is certain, but the result produced is not necessarily certain.

For example, the structure of some scene trees may change over time (case 1), but some may not (case 2). The structure of the node tree generated by using `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` and not using it may be inconsistent (case 1) or consistent (case 2). Uncertain results can be even more confusing.

The first three flags in `DuplicateFlags` are relatively independent, and the fourth flag `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` is somewhat coupled with the first three flags. The final results will be more.

`DuplicateFlags` is an extension flag. Enabling it will add the corresponding functionality, without it, `Node.duplicate()` will just fall back to the basic functionality.

> > But again, what does leaving out this flag actually achieve? The documentation only says what function it uses behind the scenes, but it leaves it completely open to interpretation what the result is.
> 
> The result is not described, but only the method used is described. This is because the method used is certain, but the result produced is not necessarily certain.
> 
> For example, the structure of some scene trees may change over time (case 1), but some may not (case 2). The structure of the node tree generated by using `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` and not using it may be inconsistent (case 1) or consistent (case 2). Uncertain results can be even more confusing.
> 
> The first three flags in `DuplicateFlags` are relatively independent, and the fourth flag `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` is somewhat coupled with the first three flags. The final results will be more.
> 
> `DuplicateFlags` is an extension flag. Enabling it will add the corresponding functionality, without it, `Node.duplicate()` will just fall back to the basic functionality.

It's essentially just a "start from clean slate if possible, but only for instances". A better name might actually be `DUPLICATE_REINSTANTIATE`. This would also be less likely to mislead people into thinking it will spit out a non-instance if omitted. Because a lack of instantiation is expected to result in a non-instance, but a lack of reinstantiation just leaves the current form intact.

I still think the documentation needs to clarify more, because even if a user knows the nuances of what `instantiate` does, it doesn't explain what should or should not be expected to happen when used by `duplicate`. Just as `owner` is not copied, it is not an unreasonable assumption that the engine would refrain from copying `scene_file_path` in certain cases. The documentation should clarify that `duplicate` will never alter whether or not something _is_ an instance.

But that is a doc thing so I will open up another issue for that and close this one, since as it stands, it is intended behaviour.

Thanks!

> Just as `owner` is not copied

The owner is copied, otherwise the `owner` of the new node is `null`.

> > Just as `owner` is not copied
> 
> The owner is copied, otherwise the `owner` of the new node is `null`.

It is null. Even if the original is not.

> It is null. Even if the original is not.

There are no nested scenes (no nodes belonging to other scenes) in your main scene. The owner of the nodes in the new scene is set only when the scene is saved.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/00a05128540016095a35eedef1a40069d50798c2/scene/main/node.cpp#L3983-L3984

Neither the `scene_file_path` nor the `owner` properties' usage have `PROPERTY_USAGE_STORAGE` set. Therefore, it's expected that they are not copied. 

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/00a05128540016095a35eedef1a40069d50798c2/scene/main/node.cpp#L3016

However, the `scene_file_path` is processed separately.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/00a05128540016095a35eedef1a40069d50798c2/scene/main/node.cpp#L2802

My note was specifically about this earlier statement: > `Node.duplicate()` copies the properties of the node. `owner` is not an exception. This is demonstrably false as a standalone statement, within or outside of the context of this bug report: It's nice to know now why it isn't copied. It can technically be debated whether or not the separate processing of `scene_file_path` should be conditional based on the `DUPLICATE_USE_INSTANTIATION` flag, but that's a separate thing, and I'm gonna just close this issue now.
